title: How Could a Man Walk 120 Years With God… and Still Leave Us Wanting More?
paragraphs: How Could a Man Walk 120 Years With God… and Still Leave Us Wanting More?
The Number Wasn’t the Miracle… His Surrender Was.
Somewhere between the desert heat and the silence of Mount Nebo, there’s a question that doesn’t sit quietly.
How do we know Moses was about 120 years old?
And maybe more unsettling than that… what did those 120 years actually look like in the eyes of God?
Because if we’re honest, most of us aren’t afraid of dying early.
We’re afraid of living long… and wasting it.
Scripture doesn’t leave Moses’ age as a mystery or legend. It confronts us with it, directly, boldly, almost uncomfortably clear:

וּמֹשֶׁה בֶּן־מֵאָה וְעֶשְׂרִים שָׁנָה בְּמֹתוֹ לֹא־כָהֲתָה עֵינוֹ וְלֹא־נָס לֵחֹה׃
“Mosheh ben-me’ah ve’esrim shanah b’moto, lo-kahatah eino, velo-nas lechoh.”
“Now Moses was one hundred and twenty years old when he died; his eye was not dim, nor his natural vigor diminished.” (Deuteronomy 34:7)
One hundred and twenty.
Not symbolic. Not exaggerated. Not poetic filler.
A number anchored in covenant history.
But here’s what grips the soul—Scripture doesn’t emphasize the number to impress us.
It reveals it to expose us.
Because Moses didn’t just live long.
He lived broken… then called… then resisted… then transformed… then surrendered.
And God counted every year.
Acts 7:23 whispers into that timeline:

Ὡς δὲ ἐπληροῦτο αὐτῷ τεσσεράκοντα ἔτη…
“When he was about forty years old…”
Forty years in Egypt.
Forty years in exile.
Forty years leading people who complained about miracles.
Three chapters of a life most people would have quit in the first paragraph.
But God didn’t waste a single season.
And neither did Moses—once he stopped running.
Because the scandal of Moses’ story isn’t that he lived to 120.
It’s that he wasn’t supposed to be the one God used.
A murderer.
A fugitive.
A man who said, “I am not eloquent.”

לֹא אִישׁ דְּבָרִים אָנֹכִי… כְּבַד־פֶּה וּכְבַד לָשׁוֹן אָנֹכִי
“Lo ish devarim anokhi… kevad-peh u’khevad lashon anokhi.”
“I am not a man of words… I am slow of speech and tongue.” (Exodus 4:10)
Yet somehow, this same man stood before Pharaoh, split seas, carried commandments, and walked so closely with God that Scripture says:

“וּמֹשֶׁה לֹא־יָדַע כִּי קָרַן עוֹר פָּנָיו”
“Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone.” (Exodus 34:29)
He didn’t even realize the glory was on him.
And maybe that’s the point.
The world measures years.
God measures surrender.
You can live 30 years and be finished in the Spirit…
Or live 120 and still be burning with purpose.
Moses didn’t die because he aged out.
He died because his assignment was complete.
Let that sit heavier than you expected.
Because some of us are praying for longer life…
While God is asking for deeper obedience.
And here’s where it turns personal.
You’ve been counting time.
God’s been counting moments of surrender.
You remember your failures.
God remembers your turning point.
You think your past disqualifies you.
Moses would disagree.
No… heaven would disagree.
Because Moses’ life doesn’t prove how long a man can live.
It proves how completely a broken man can be rewritten.
And if you feel like your timeline is messy… delayed… wasted…
Then you’re exactly where Moses was… before everything changed.
So be honest.
Not polished.
Not religious.
Honest.
Because silence is where shame survives.
But confession is where grace begins to breathe again.
And someone you know needs to read this.
Someone who thinks it’s too late.
Not randomly.
Specifically.
Because sharing this isn’t just content.
It’s calling.
And if your heart is serious about growing deeper in Jesus Christ, there’s more waiting for you than just posts.
Not to sell you something…
But to surround your life with reminders that you belong to Christ.
If this message stirred something in you, don’t ignore it.
Honor it.
Support it.
Because glorifying God isn’t passive.
It’s participation.
And this… this is one way you step into it.
Moses lived 120 years…
But eternity remembers him for one thing—
He finally said yes.
